Welcome to Competitive Innovations, our weekly feature for a number of game lines across the tabletop wargame space. Each week our army list and tactics experts canvass the top tournaments for their game of specialty, looking at the week’s top match-ups and how they played out on the tabletop to let you know what’s hot, what’s not, and what might be coming next as the competitive meta evolves year-round.

Apologies for the wait folks, it's a pretty packed week this week! As we move toward the Las Vegas Open, the big one, people are getting as many games in as they can before the big event. This week we're hitting 5 events from all over the world.

Another positive note is the size of these events continue to climb, which shows a huge shift from Ghyran. The people seem to love Aqshy, and that's great news!

Thoughts

Given this is one of the earliest weeks we've gotten to see the Ogor book in action as they've been in a bit of purgatory waiting for the official release and I can see how a skilled KO player with the right list could manage a strong win.

They have great abilities for being able to engage at long distance. Ogors want to be able to charge, or force their opponents into a less than ideal charge against them. If they can't do that, a lot of their abilities are neutered pretty hard and KO can keep their distance to dog the Ogors with their pretty mediocre saves by gunning them down with strong ranged weapons.

title: TheChirurgeon's Road Through 2026, Part 38: Days 1-2 of Challenger's Cup
content:
Welcome back, Dear Reader, to my ongoing blog of hobby and competitive play progress through 2026. Last week I was doing some final prep for Salt Lake City. And by "final prep" i mean "playing a lot of HeroQuest," though I did get in one extremely important practice game against my friend Andrew Corban on Labor Day. Anyways, this week I'm talking about the 2026 Challengers Cup. This is ostensibly four days of Warhammer - two travel days and three days of games - so I'm going to talk about Thursday and Friday today and then tomorrow I'll be back with an extra instalment to talk about days two and three of the event and the trip back. This will hopefully let me get a bit more "travel diary" about things and let some of the prose breathe. or something.

Anyways, here's ten thousand words about my Warhammer vacation with the boys.

Thursday: The Boys Return to Town

There are a limited number of direct flights from IAH to SLC every day, so I had to leave around midday and fly back Monday morning. That effectively turns this into a five-day event, which is a lot, especially if you aren't blessed with the boon of working from home and largely being able to just work from the airport and/or plane.

Also pictured (left to right): Erik Nelson, T Chambliss, Andrew Corban, and David Miracle

As luck would have it, I was on the same flight to Salt Lake City as Sanctum, the Houston team of local degenerates which makes up a large portion of my regular play group. We sat in the terminal and talked for a while, grabbing beers until it was time to board. Then our flight was delayed for mechanical reasons and we were deplaned. Then we were delayed due to lightning strikes - the tarmac shuts down when there's visible lightning in the area to protect workers - for another hour or so before we finally set out.

Once I arrived in Salt Lake City, I just had to wait for James "Boon" Kelling to pick me up - he'd rented a car. We had a great location for this event: 15 minutes from the airport, 15 minutes from the venue, which meant we could get away with a single car and make round trips to the venue/airport and back. Speaking of which...

The Team House

The house itself was a large house meant for ski trips. Whenever you do these 8-man team events, you always have two big challenges:

  1. The car. Unless you rent a bus or full size van, nothing is going to seat eight of you, especially once you start factoring in the space needed for armies and miniature cases. This usually means you have to rent two cars. Or do what we did and make two trips every time you go somewhere.
  2. The house. Finding a house which can sleep eight people who don't want to share a bed is nearly impossible. Even with big houses, you're usually talking four or five bedrooms at most, and maybe a couch or two. Which usually means someone has to sleep on the floor unless you have a lot of couches and/or fold-out beds.

When I book a house for something like this I'm usually looking for 5 bedrooms and 3 couches, or a fold-out bed or two. I also tend to focus on getting a decent kitchen and making sure we have a grill at the house. The grill makes cooking meals a lot easier, and one of the things I emphasize at teams events is doing big family-style dinners with cooked meals. We eat healthier, we eat cheaper, and we eat as a team.

This particular house had a solid grill and a great back patio with some truly amazing views. The landscape out in Salt Lake City is absolutely something, and it's a bit surreal when you're walking around and surrounded by mountains. On our way back to the house we stopped at the grocery store to do our preliminary grocery run. This is one of my favorite parts of any team or group vacation: I love planning meals and doing the grocery run. I feel like the quartermaster whenever I hit the grocery store on that initial run, sending runners to different aisles, investigating meat and picking fruit, doing it in absurd quantities - MY BOYS GOTTA EAT.

Dinner our first night was burgers and dogs. I biffed this a bit, in that Chase is a vegetarian and I didn't account for that, but he made do with the large variety of snacks, fruits, and vegetables on the first night, then on the second night we picked up some quick substitutions for him to ensure we had proper coverage. Burgers and dogs are usually my night 1 go-to; they're quick and easy, just do the burgs about 7 minutes per side on the grill with some salt and pepper, maybe some Montreal steak seasoning and worcestershire sauce if you wanna get fancy, and heat the dogs while you heat up some chili and cheese. Flip the burgers once.

We waited up for our final team member, Wallace, to arrive, and had a proper reunion chat and some beer before calling it a night. We spend some time on the porch and talk about lists, look at our round 1 pairing, and talk theory. As it turns out, Chase is a sicko who loves to do pairings, which is GREAT, because I hate doing pairings. I'm purely a vibes guy. And so is Chase, actually - he's just way better at it than I am. I end up crashing around midnight, with a dessert which consisted of "a fistful of pepto bismol."

Meet the Team

The Tabletop Battles team is not a traditional team for this kind of event; most of these teams are located near each other, or have players who can regularly practice. Our team is spread out all over, and no two players in our group have the ability to regularly play in person. This means we have zero hours of practice as a group, and have to largely rely on player skill to get through our matchups. the good news is, we're all at least decent players, and some of us are very good. Here's the rundown of the team we fielded this year, which is mostly the same as last year, but with two substitutions.

Robert "TheChirurgeon" Jones

Thousand Sons - Purge the Foe

Hey, it's me! I was ostensibly team captain of this outfit, but I handed those duties over to chase pretty quickly. My list for this event was pretty bad - designed to get Thousand Sons on Purge the Foe and pull off some bullshit tricks - more on that in a bit. I've been playing for a while, and just started elevating my game to winning GTs and attending WCW for the first time last year. I've done about half a dozen teams events now, including last year's Challengers Cup.

Chase "Gunum" Garber

Emperor's Children - Disruption

Chase was supposed to be on our team last year, but injured his hands pretty badly doing gardening work and had to take about half a year off of Warhammer as a result. He's one of the game's better list builders and an absolute pervert when it comes to doing pairings - he loves doing them, and basically cook over as team captain once we arrived at the event. Chase was running a very off-meta Emperor's Children army, focused on Flawless Blades.

James "Boon" Kelling

Aeldari - Priority Assets

Probably the most accomplished single player on the Tabletop Battles team, James has a long history of awards and strong play, having finished in the top 20 of the ITC multiple times and having won a World Championship in 2022 by taking down Andrew Gonyo in the Best Overall bracket. James has recently lost a bit of a step thanks to the selfish decision to "have children," but is always dangerous as he's just an incredibly smart player on the table.

Campbell "srm" McLaughlin

Space Marines - Take and Hold

Campbell is in a wonderful position of being a former casual/narrative player who has since been comp-pilled and as of last year, teampilled. Campbell is on Space Marines, and while his first competitive love are Black Templars, he's currently being forced to play Ultramarines for our team. He's on a list that uses Librarius Conclave and will likely end up having to take on Custodes in most of our matchups.

Shane Watts

Chaos Daemons - Take and Hold

Shane is another venerable veteran of the competitive scene, and was on last year's Ottawa and Challengers Cup teams. Shane's moved on from his Votann, and has recently been playing a Plague Legion list that specializes in battle-shocking you far past any notions of reason or restraint. He's packing a Sloppity Bilepiper because few things are as satisfying as killing Ghazghkull from a single failed Leadership test at -2.

Thomas "Goatboy" Reidy

World Eaters - Purge the Foe

Goatboy is back on the team this year for Challengers Cup, and he's once again packing World Eaters. Goatboy is one of my favorite people in this hobby, and he's a delight to have on the team. He's been on World Eaters for a while now, and was also playing them back in January during the LVO Teams Tournament. His list is Berzerker Horde; he's not about the fancy triple detachment tricks or running lots of Terminators.

Craig "MasterSlowPoke" Sniffen

Orks - Priority Assets

Our resident Rainbow Warriors sicko, MasterSlowPoke has recently been building an Orks army following the release of 11th edition. With the Codex out and legal for this event, he's well positioned to play one of the game's best armies, and we're super invested in having a top meta army or two in our team roster. The big challenge is that Craig has played exactly zero games with his army before this event. But when you have flash gitz, that shouldn't matter, right?

Wallace O'Donnell

Chaos Knights - Reconnaissance

Wallace is a chill dude and a lifesaver as far as I'm concerned. Last year he saved our asses by joining last minute after we had a drop, and he did the same thing this year after we had a player drop from the event with just a few weeks to go. That level of frustration normally makes my desire to do 8 man events bottom out, but I'm always happy to include Wallace, who's not only good for it, but an absolute list building genius who always comes up with cool shit. He's a very underrated player.

Ok, it's not an ideal list. The idea here is that I'm taking Warpmeld Pact purely to get Purge the Foe while leaving space for the Ritual of Regeneration Detachment, which is where the real value comes from. Being able to bring back dead Terminators and Rubrics is huge, and the Stratagem to essentially grenade a unit you're in combat with is massive for being able to survive combats against elite infantry and keep your units around. It's also crucial when you don't have a fall back and shoot/fight stratagem.

Other key tricks in this Detachment pair:

  • The Tzaangor Shaman with Eruption of Vitality can get back up on death - and doesn't count as a new unit when he does so. This makes him great for being my Beacon unit, since he can die, get back up, and score the secondary. I can also use the Gift of Change Stratagem on him when he dies to make a Chaos Spawn, then he can get back up, and make another Chaos Spawn when he dies the second time. Which is hilarious.
  • The two Scarab bricks can dish out a ton of hurt but do tend to but up against each other as only one can really use the re-rolls/AP buffs at a time. That said, the redundancy is important.
  • The Forgefiends do good damage and support the Scarabs - the idea is to use them to give enemy units -2 to hit and -1 to wound a unit of Scarabs, keeping them on the table.
  • The Mutalith Vortex beast can advance and charge or advance and shoot with the Touched by Tzeentch Stratagem.
  • The Tzaangors can go back into reserves, then deep strike 6" away from enemy units using the Twisted Mirage Stratagem, which forces an opponent to screen me out at 6" late game or let me sneak in to score free points.

It's not amazing. It's barely functional. But it scores for killing things, and it's good at killing things. It's got decent movement, and some nasty board control overwatch. This is not a 20-0 Defender list; I barely care about the terrain layout. This is a 10-10 list designed to win close games or keep things manageable against a wide variety of lists. I'm going to be the attacker this time, and getting thrown on grenades with a hope of keeping things close.

I pair into John Kilcommons, running Lions of the Emperor Custodes. This list will more or less be in every team we play and I'm not the ideal partner for it; it runs three Terminator bricks to my two and that makes it hard for me to get the upper hand unless I'm going second.

Unfortunately, I'm going first. So my goal is to play very cagey and not let him get off any turn 1 charges with his army. I need to stay out of melee as long as possible. I score easy Display of Might turn 1 and work on staying ahead on primary all game but it's hard to do do that for most Purge missions these days, especially going first.

So very little happens the first two turns, then we start mixing it up. I end up dropping in the middle and controlling the center of the board for most of the game, but the Allarus are a big problem whenever they collide with my units. The big money moment in this game comes when I Overwatch John's Shield Captain to death with a lucky shot from my Forgefiend, and then he fails to get back up on death, buying me a huge swing in win probability.

Unfortunately while I stay ahead a few points on primary most of the game, John just outdraws me on secondaries, especially on rounds 3-4. I'm ahead going into the final turn but John draws what he needs to pull out the win with Cleanse for 2, giving him an 83-82 win. I kept this one close in a way that makes me pretty happy, but I'd have liked to score 11 or 12.

Those extra points would have helped, because we'd end up in a close tie with their team, pulling an 83-77 draw; two more points and we'd have had the W. Still, we're not upset about starting with a draw - we're undefeated, after all.

John was a fun opponent and we played a tight game with some crazy swings in both directions. I enjoyed it quite a bit and we had a good time. Great opponent.

Lunch is a mad dash to the food trucks outside. The lines are long and the sun is brutal. I decide to avoid sitting in line by ordering via QR code from the burrito truck. They run out of food and I wait a full hour before going to them to cancel my order. At that point I go to the next truck and ask for the fastest thing they have, which turns out to be birria potstickers.

They were delicious, and sorely needed at this point. I was flagging after a long day, and those dumplings saved my life.

The heavy bolters are bad news for my 2W units, and to make matters worse, Trevor is on Priority Assets, which is a rough matchup for Purge, especially if you go second. I need to maintain control of the center objectives to keep Trevor from repeatedly scoring for his dropped markers.

I can't afford to play super cagey on this one; I need to hold the middle to prevent scoring. Things start off OK for me, but I make a big blunder: Trevor comes out quickly early to try and kill my Beacon-holding Tzaangor Shaman. My plan: Let him die, turn him into a spawn, then use the spawn to block a charge into the Shaman. I forgot of course that the Spawn has a 5+ Feel No Pain however, and he gets shot to death - barely, to the wound - by the sisters who were in the Immolator. As a result, Trevor can charge and tank shock the Shaman, and when he does he spikes the dice and gets 5 wounds off, killing the Shaman.

That was a tough mistake on my end, and one I won't make again. Trevor spends most of the game feeding me units piecemeal, but is able to break things open after I have a disastrous melee turn against his Sacresants. The Scarabs charged in, dropped 21 attacks with swords, connected with exactly five of them, and ended up killing only two models. They then murdered half the unit, and that was a backbreaker I couldn't afford.

Trevor's Sacresants stayed untouchable most of the game, constantly crushing their saves. Trevor also got off another two critical tank shocks, doing 5 damage each time on 10 dice. Going first was a brutal punishment here, ensuring I'd also get bodied on the final turn for some additional points after I failed to kill a vehicle or Ephrael Stern on the final turn, missing out out some crucial points. If I'd had those, this could have been a close game, but as it was, I ended up losing 6-14. Not my favorite game by outcome, but Trevor was a great opponent and we had a good time.

The good news is that we tied again, 82-78. At this point we were pretty happy with our UNDEFEATED result, and joking about going 0-0-6 for the event; the ultimate "friendmaker" score.

We do our two trips back and grab a few missing grocery items this time around. Friday night is TACO NIGHT at the house. We cook up about 3 lbs of hamburger with taco seasoning, then add shredded cheese, lettuce, diced tomatoes, sour cream, Spanish rice, and refried beans to the mix, plus a good mix of corn tortillas and hard shells. To top things off, I made some of my extremely creamy guacamole. The general recipe here is:

  • 6 avocados
  • 1 diced tomato
  • half a clove of finely chopped garlic
  • 1/3 a red onion, small diced
  • salt
  • pepper
  • lime juice
  • a fistful of cilantro
  • paprika
  • cumin

I tend to err on the creamier side with my guac, and it turned out really well. We certainly finished the night with none left, which is always a good sign. Tacos are a great pick for a dinner at these things; you can buy most of the ingredients pre-made, and they allow players to kind of build however they want, making it easy to just put out ingredients and let people go to town. Because we're finishing kind of late even with two-round days, dinner can run late. So you ideally want meals which don't take a long time to cook.

The spread itself was solid:

It was a crazy amount of taco meat, but the good news is we had plenty left over for breakfast tacos the next morning. I think I had something like eight tacos and we had plenty of food left after that. Overall a very solid night and a great cap to a great first day for the event. We'd hang out and drink beer and talk for a while, recap the day, and talk about tomorrow's opponents for a while. I crashed around midnight.

Final Thoughts

OK, that wraps up days 1 and 2. Tomorrow I'll be back with the second half of this report. recapping days 2 and 3 of the event and our final results. See you then.

title: How to Paint Everything: Napoleonic Polish
content:
So you've seen the movie and now you know with absolute certainty where Napoleon went wrong. You can, and will, do better. It's time to get into real wargaming. Welcome to Napoleonics.

This article is part of our Getting Started: Napoleonics guide.

Whilst not a major power during the Napoleonic era, the Poles were some of the most dedicated of Napoleon's foreign forces. Seeing the Emperor as their best bet for lasting independence following the Partitions, Polish soldiers served throughout his campaigns.

Our guide covers two of the most recognizable uniforms of the Polish forces of the time - that of the Legion of the Vistula and the Duchy of Warsaw.

The Legion of the Vistula

Formed in 1807, the Legion of the Vistula served the French forces in the Peninsular War, the invasion of Russia, and the War of the Sixth Coalition. It was made up of infantry and cavalry, with the infantry organized into six company battalions as per the French organization put in place in February 1808.

Their most distinct piece of equipment was the czapka, a square-topped variant of the shako, which became a regular part of Polish uniforms of the era (although historians continue to debate how widespread it actually was, since Polish uniforms tended to be a mix of salvaged Prussian, Austrian, and French uniforms).

Art of Polish soldiers wearing the czapka. (Credit - "Polish Uhlans from the Duchy of Warsaw 1807-1815", by J Suchodolski, 1852)

To build my miniatures, I used the Elite Companies, French infantry 1807-1814 box from Perry Miniatures, along with the Vistula Legion heads from Warlord Games (which come in Fusilier, Voltigeur, and Grenadier varieties). I chose this set for its more dynamic poses, as I originally built my models to play Silver Bayonet.

I used the following Warhammer Paints when painting my Legion of the Vistula force:

  • White Scar Spray (this can be replaced with Wraithbone if you wish)
  • White Scar (this can be replaced with Wraithbone if you wish)
  • Apothecary White Contrast
  • Guilliman Flesh Contrast
  • Iyanden Yellow Contrast
  • Talassar Blue Contrast
  • Black Templar Contrast
  • Abaddon Black
  • Mournfang Brown
  • Leadbelcher
  • Retributor Armour
  • Word Bearers Red
  • Zandri Dust
  • Ushabti Bone
  • Nuln Oil

So the first stage was to prime and undercoat my model. I used Jenolite Universal Etch Primer, and then used White Scar spray for the basecoat since the Vistula Legion uses bright colors. After that, I covered the whole model with Apothecary White Contrast - which shaded all the white belts, straps, and trousers, as well as helping me make out the model's details for the following stages. Once that was dry, I applied Guilliman Flesh Contrast (though any similar contrast such as Darkoath Flesh would also work) to the face and hands of the model.

With that done, I moved onto the uniform colors - starting with carefully painting the lapel beneath the crossed straps with Iyanden Yellow. Take care not to spill over onto the straps or coat - but if you do, just wait for it all to dry before applying some White Scar to the spill to cover it up. The next step was the coat - which I did with Talassar Blue contrast. Then I used Black Templar contrast for the hat, shoes, and scabbard.

From here on, I switched to regular paints for the details. First, I used Mournfang Brown to paint the musket, pack, and pouches on the model. Then, I applied Leadbelcher to the upper half of the musket and bayonet, as well as the dagger handle on the back. The other metallic I used was used Retributor Armour, for the front plate of the hat and the dagger guard. The hat pom and dagger tassel were painted with Word Bearers Red, and the musket strap was painted with Zandri Dust.

The next step was basing - which consisted of a basecoat of Mournfang Brown, followed by a drybrush of Zandri Dust, and then a drybrush of Ushabti Bone. Finally, I checked the model for any small spills and mistakes and tidied it up with the paints I had already used as necessary before giving it a wash of Nuln Oil. Once that was dry, I used Abaddon Black to paint the rim of the base, and just like that, it was table ready!

The Duchy of Warsaw

The army of the Duchy of Warsaw saw action across the continent - the 4th & 7th Infantry Regiments marched at Talavera in 1809, whilst the 8th took part in the Austro-Polish War of the same year. For this I used the Perry Miniatures Napoleonic Duchy of Warsaw Infantry Elite Companies 1807-14, and settled on painting up the uniform of the 7th, to use alongside my Vistula Legion in Peninsular games. Interestingly, painting the 4th would be very similar to painting the Vistula Legion, just with red collars, red cuffs, and red edging to the yellow lapel, and a slightly darker blue for the coat!

I used the following Warhammer Paints:

  • White Scar Spray (this can be replaced with Wraithbone if you wish)
  • White Scar (this can be replaced with Wraithbone if you wish)
  • Apothecary White Contrast
  • Darkoath Flesh Contrast
  • Leviadon Blue Contrast
  • Blood Angels Red Contrast
  • Black Templar Contrast
  • Abaddon Black
  • Mournfang Brown
  • Leadbelcher
  • Retributor Armour
  • Word Bearers Red
  • Zandri Dust
  • Ushabti Bone
  • Nuln Oil Wash

The first few stages (priming, undercoating, and painting the flesh) I did exactly the same way as I did in the Vistula Legion guide above. The big difference is in the uniform colors - I used Leviadon Blue for the coat, and Blood Angels Red for the lapel. In case of spillage, I used White Scar to tidy up the white on the trousers and straps again!

Then, again just the same way as for the Vistula Legion, I used Mournfang Brown to paint the musket stock and pack, followed by Black Templar Contrast on the czapka and the shoes, again making use of White Scar to tidy up if necessary. Then it was time for details - I used Leadbelcher on the upper half of the musket and the whole bayonet, and added a dash of Retributor Armour on the hat plate over and under the white cord. The pom was done with Word Bearers Red.

To paint the base, I used Mournfang Brown as a basecoat, and then drybrushed Zandri Dust and then Ushabti Bone over the top in lighter layers. Finally, I washed the whole model with Nuln Oil to darken and shade it. The finish may end up somewhat glossy, but this can be resolved by using a matt acrylic varnish, which will also protect your models (I use Humbrol Acrylic Varnish spray).

Credit: Hydriatus

Of course, this is just the 7th Regiment - depending on the regiment and soldier you're working on (such as grenadiers, fusiliers, or voltigeurs), the poms, cuffs, collar and epaulettes would be colored differently!

But that's it! Variations on these schemes make up the majority of the uniforms of the Polish forces during the Napoleonic era - if you have any particular tips and tricks of your own, why not share them in the comments?

title: MTG's first Reality Fracture commander deck gives Magic's unluckiest character a second chance
content:
Dack Fayden, greatest thief in the multiverse, the planeswalker protagonist of the Magic the Gathering comics series, is one of the unluckiest characters in the franchise. Lots of characters have died, but poor Fayden was killed in the trailer for War of the Spark, and his death in the tie-in novel was described second-hand. But in the Echoverse he's alive and well - and his newly revealed Multiverse Reforged commander deck looks like a lot of fun.

Admittedly, this version of Fayden isn't a planeswalker. Dack Fayden, Helping Hand, is a 4/6 legendary human advisor who costs two white and four generic mana. And he just wants to help! When Fayden enters, you reveal cards from the top of your library until you've revealed one creature for each opponent, put them all into play, goad them for the rest of the game, and then give each one to a different opponent.

Dack Fayden is an auto-include for the admittedly small pool of players running Zedruu the Greathearted. This Jeskai commander donates creatures to opponents, letting you draw more cards and gain more life each turn, the more of your creatures they control. Fayden will play perfectly into that deck's strategy of giving your opponent cards with downside for profit..

As the creatures Fayden summons enter under your control before they pass to an opponent, you can also harvest the advantage of their ETB effects. The safe way to do that is to go with creatures with good ETBs and bad stat lines - a Witch Enchanter destroys an opponent's Sol Ring when it enters, and then it's just a vanilla 2/2 when your opponent gets it.

Or you could run good creatures, and treat Fayden's donation as a loan arrangement. As Fayden goads them, you're safe from their attacks until you only have one opponent left in play - at which point you can use Oblivion Ring effects to temporarily exile them, then let them re-enter the battlefield under your control. If you use an actual O-ring you'll need a way to sacrifice it, but Crack in Time, Battle at the Helvault, and Morningtide's Light are all temporary exile effects that don't stick around forever. And if you're also running blue, then Coveted Falcon, Venser the Sojourner, and Become Anonymous all have ways to reclaim cards that you own but don't control.

Powerful? Doesn't seem like it, but quite entertainingly silly! Which cards from Multiverse Reforged and the main Reality Fracture MTG set are you most keen to build around? Let us know in the Wargamer Discord community!

title: Commander Focus: Pia, Aether Ascetic, Erosion, & Jyoti, Moag Ancient
content:
Erosion is one of perhaps the most fascinating natural phenomena that you can observe with the naked eye. Whether it’s the strange outcroppings and boulders suspended in America’s deserts, or the River Rhine tracing its form from the Alps to the North Sea, in ways both grandiose and minuscule the wear on our world is always visible. Erosion affects different materials differently, however, leading to strange columns of sandstone, or jutting diversion of a stream, and when the base layer of any given material grows weak enough the winds & waters will take the path of least resistance, pushing through once-solid stone, or settled sands. This is an article about erosion, not in the geological sense, but in Magic, and in Commander—this is about the simplification of tutor chains, and wear of enamel caps on the grinding teeth of this game. This is about Pia, Aether Ascetic. Pia’s one of the most exciting cards to arrive in Reality Fracture, and in a set rife with flashy Mythic Sphinges, colorshifted spins on competitive staples, and literal Tarmogoyf. Her effect is fairly simple: When she enters, you can pitch a card and search an Enchantment. This would be strong on a White or Black card, certainly, as tutors can smooth combo decks’ lines and allow toolbox strategies to find the pieces they need at the right time, but Pia is only as exciting as she is because...she’s Green. Not only is she the very first Enchantment tutor that has a Color identity of Monogreen (which isn’t an overcosted omnitutor), Pia also comes in at a cool 3 mana, being fairly inexpensive to weave into lines. So inexpensive, and so accessible, in fact, that she’s already begun to erode the limestone walls between known combos, and playability. The density of Green’s Creature Tutor suite is such that in any Gx deck without White/Black, you can just about find a given Enchantment as well or better than if you were in a color dedicated to finding the card type. There’s a critique which comes to mind, from FIRE Design-era Magic, that ‘Green can do anything, so long as it’s on a Creature’, and that feels eerily true here. With all that out of the way, let’s take the path of least resistance, and smooth our way towards Simic Enchantment combos, with a Commander newly-invigorated by Pia’s printing: Jyoti, Moag Ancient.

"Search your library for an enchantment card..."

Prior to the reveal of Pia, the best way to find Enchantments in something like Simic or Temur was by way of Intuition piles, where you’d choose the card you actually want, and two means of getting it back in hand. This could be your standard Regrowth, but as time’s gone on more flexible options like Bala Ged Recovery & Dryad’s Revival came along. There's a crop of issues that this previous path had though, least of all being the price tag (for some) and Game Changer status (for all) when it comes to Intuition. Things got a bit better once Gifts Ungiven was unbanned, but that's another Game Changer, whose opportunity cost was far from negligible to include. For this reason, Commanders whose win conditions were derived from Enchantments essentially needed to be White, Black, or potentially Red, if you intended to use a Reality Scramble build alongside things like Role tokens. If you were Simic, finding an Intruder Alarm or Food Chain was down to overpaying for something like Reweave as a worse-than Scramble enabler, or starting at B3 with Intuition. There's a host of Commanders this stymied, but the two I want to call out specifically are Berta, Wise Extrapolator as well as our focus today, of Jyoti.

She's Ghirapur's mayor, she's everyone's mayor.

Each of these, in spite of very minimal mechanical crossover, function as incredibly similar cards in my mind. Each goes close-to infinite with a single Enchantment, and fully infinite with access to some third piece that has ample redundancy. For Berta, Intruder Alarm and her constantly activating for X=0 leads to a repeatable action of creating a 0/0 Fractal, it dying immediately, and her untapping; this doesn't lead anywhere on its own, but alongside any number of cards which care about tokens entering, Creatures dying, etc it presents a pretty quick win. Jyoti's a bit more resilient, because she functionally produces mana and scales with being removed, but is definitely slower to win. The Elemental loves to see a Food Chain, which can (alongside the Dryad Arbor tokens produced per cast) gets close to infinite casts of your Commander, if you can somehow reduce the price tag of Commander Tax, create additional tokens, or provide your board Haste (such that the Arbor Elves can tap before being fed into the woodchipper). In either case, looking at decklists for them on Moxfield & Archidekt currently include these powerful cards, but no compelling ways to find them. In that sense, each falls victim to one of the least-fun things a combo deck can be, for all parties involved: Inconsistent. If you open your combo piece, congrats, you're threatening a win way ahead of schedule, and will be evaluated by the table as such in future games with the deck. If you don't, however, you're playing far more of a midrange game, but being focused down as though you were a combo deck. Adding consistency to either of these strategies not only increases the power floor for the deck in a given game, but also dodges these social woes which might otherwise mar one's experience with the Commander. This article's on Jyoti, but many of the lessons shown off can be equally applied to Berta.

Jyo-ti the World

So, Jyoti—what's the actual gameplan? Step one is fairly simple: Find Pia, Aether Ascetic, and use her to find one of two-ish Enchantments, being Rhystic Study or Food Chain. Step two is to get out Jyoti, and use her as a bit of ramp, maybe double up on a Landfall trigger in a given turn, before then finding a way to get her off of the field. This can be via Food Chain, if we feel the combo is close-enough at hand as to make Rhystic Study not high enough value, or something like an Altar, being Ashnod's Altar & Phyrexian Altar. These have the added bonus of being mechanisms to get Pia off the field, at which point we can do things like get her back from the graveyard to replay, or even jam a Body Double. Where things get dicey is the next part, because the path the deck takes when you're actually trying to combo off varies wildly based on available tools. If you're making extra Creatures to toss away from Food Chain when cycling through Jyoti ETBs, such as with Springheart Nantuko, then you only need a single Enchantment tutor really to get going—though it is immensely funny Nantuko is able to be found via Pia and our Creature tutors. What an accessible little gentleman. There's also the option of creating the opportunity for your Arbor Elves to tap for mana, such as via Lightning Greaves, Shang-Chi, Master of Kung Fu, or Concordant Crossroads. There is a fourth option there, in Thousand-Year Elixir, but with it being a bit expensive at 3 mana and not tutorable with what we'd want to play, it's been cut. What remains is either extremely accessible (Shang-Chi's a Creature, Crossroads is an Enchantment) or extremely good. Finally, Commander Tax. This is normally {2} on top of the existing cost, meaning that with Food Chain, Jyoti at a baseline produces 1 fewer mana than she rises in price, with the extra Dryad Arbor token made per cast. Therefore, you begin to break even once you do things like allow them to tap for mana, or make additional tokens, but another mechanism now enabled by Pia is in reducing the Tax to {1}...or less.

They call it the Simic Combine because you combine things and-

This is by way of Myth Unbound, my favorite card you're probably not playing in enough decks. This sees play in nearly all Partner brews including Green, but for Jyoti, what it does is much the same as our other enablers, with the added bonus of drawing a card every cycle. It also makes use of another subtheme in the deck: Enchantment clones. We're on essentially all options available to Simic to copy Enchantments, from the obvious like Copy Enchantment itself, and Estrid's Invocation, to more peculiar paths like Moritte of the Frost & Flash Photography. This is in service of two things: Generating a truly insurmountable amount of value ala cEDH by copying a Rhystic Study, or doubling up on a combo enabler, such as Myth Unbound. This can even be things like Springheart Nantuko, or Leyline of Abundance, allowing all these pieces to serve as 'wild cards' in terms of our endgame. Better yet, you can usually also target your opponent's Enchantments, meaning we're far less liable to groan at a Rhystic without one of our own.

Mamma Pia!

A Dancing Queen, often seen, should have been printed in the 20-teens.

The die is cast, and our gameplan is fully explained, but how consistent is it? Well...Green has perhaps the best suite of tutors in the game, following closely behind Black, although in their majority the best options aren't Game Changers. Moreover, unlike Black, a lot of these tools toss the searched-for Creature onto the battlefield directly, leaving less room for countermagic. Chord of Calling, Green Sun's Zenith, & Nature's Rhythm are the big ones, with X=3 being the common pick. To that end, usually following the Jyoti turn where we've ramped twice, these are our next play. They can of course find Pia, but also cards like Lotus Cobra or Badgermole Cub as additional acceleration, or Savvy Trader to not only help Jyoti cycle faster but also reset a dead Pia/Mystic Remora. There's also tutors to hand, like Sylvan & Worldly Tutor, and Time of Need, which keys off of the fact that Pia is indeed Legendary. Also played are Neoform & Eldritch Evolution, one-time Birthing Pod effects which get us from things like our mana dorks into Pia, Pia into Savvy Trader, or Jyoti into Moritte.

This deck has a whopping ~16 paths to Pia, and Pia herself then opens up the rest of the cards we want to see. That's a cool ~80% to see Pia or a means to her in our first opening 8 cards, and counting the mulligan, 96%. That's a rate higher than even many 'Secret Commander' lists, whose entire purpose is to hinge the deck around a card not in the Command Zone. Turns out that Green being able to do or find anything so long as it passes through the elephant-sized needle's eye that is 'Creatures' makes for obscenely consistent tutor chains. The actual win comes from casting Jyoti (or Eternal Scourge) enough times to amass a big enough board, and then flex Concordant Crossroads to provide haste and swing out for lethal...made easier by something like the new Roiling Canopy, which results in a massive Jyoti to pump up our board. Simple, clean, compact, and able to be reset via Endurance if things get stuck in the yard..

Example Decklist: Jyoti, Chandra's Step-Sister

There's something that I want to touch on here, which is that the ramp package here isn't what you'd expect for a deck that has a 4 mana Commander, much less one which actually ramps you. Why wouldn't we be playing all the 2-mana ramp spells that allow us to do the 2-4-6 ramp chain that's become so common? For starters, Jyoti isn't necessarily a card we aim to play especially early, as we don't appreciate paying 6 for her after a board wipe; the Dryad Arbor tokens have a tendency to get caught in the crossfire of things, so we'd much rather run out value engines like Faerie Mastermind or similar, then plan to play Jyoti after our tutor chain is live. Therefore, my preference is in playing 1-mana dorks, like Delighted Halfling, as one of the luxuries Green is afforded compared to other colors. We're also on a few ways to pick up our Commander, should our combo be interrupted after casting her 20+ times, being Road of Return & Command Beacon. A lot of the tools used by Prossh, Skyraider of Kher (the OG Food Chain Commander) come home to roost here, but Jyoti's cheaper, more resilient, and has access to Rhystic.

Decklists are kept updated, and may change with set releases.

In terms of Bracket, part of why this Commander Focus is on Jyoti and not Berta is the fact that I'm not comfortable denying the fact Berta's a bit fast for Bracket 3. Prior to the printing of Pia, the combo was inconsistent enough as to not require we forcibly scale her up to B4...but now, being able to play 15-20 ways of chaining to Intruder Alarm means Jyoti is far more apt for the Bracket. Even so, the fact you'll have games where you copy Rhystic Study is cooler than what Berta'd be doing anyway, and I'm a sucker for Myth Unbound as a core piece of one's list. This can be pushed to Bracket 4, but to be quite honest a lot of B2 lists running Command Zone combos with Pia shouldn't even look at Bracket 2. Now there's no longer the shield of inconsistency to protect less powerful lists, and for that reason I'm less keen on powering down Jyoti, unless your intent is to kill via combat by boosting her with a Tifa Lockheart or Mightform Harmonizer.

Not Yugioh (Yet)

Alex Stone lends elegance to the MH3 portrait arts, even without a head to focus on.

Reality Fracture is a set which takes big swings, and Pia is certainly part of that. We've seen some absolutely heinous designs deployed in the set, at a greater density than any since probably Final Fantasy, and that's still a maybe. Entomb but for Lands, High Tide but for Mountains, and of course, Green's first Enchantment tutor. This is a powerful set, and one I'll likely spend time diving into far beyond its release, especially with Star Trek thus far not inspiring confidence. In spite of all this power, I don't think Pia will be "problematic", even with my erosion metaphor, for the majority of the playerbase; where she's most obscene is in lists built by the Johnny-Spikes of the world, with combos planned two or even three steps ahead in the chain. For the majority of players, it'll be 'Oh sweet, I can tutor Rhystic Study!', and while that is certainly a problem it's not one of Pia, but of her targets. If anything, this might be part of what gets Food Chain back onto the Game Changers list, as it was recently relieved of its position. The thought there, per the committee, was that 'If you're playing Food Chain, you should be able to self-regulate', and I feel that downplays both the rising competence of the wider Commander community, and their self-control. For as much as I'm an advocate for deeply weird, cool combo decks, I'm also here to preach that cards like Food Chain, Yuriko, Urza, and even Ashnod's Altar should be Game Changers. Greater regulation by the letter of the law, and not the intent or vibe, is how we keep cards like Pia and sets like Reality Fracture from feeling like powercreep as opposed to added fun. Yugioh's long-since eroded the columns holding apart any two cards, and while our Aether Ascetic is a step in that direction, there's still plenty of sandbar left to chew through until all combos are intertwined.

Until next time, I can still hear you saying you would never break the chain.

title: [Kill Team] Tactical Focus: Murderwing
content:
In this series of Kill Team articles we take a deep dive into one of the available teams, analyzing each team's strengths and weaknesses, how to set up important plays, and ultimately what to consider to pilot the team to victory. Note that this article assumes you already have knowledge of the basic rules for each team, and will reference abilities and ploys from that team throughout. If you want to learn more about the rules for each team you can find the most up to date version of the rules on the Warhammer Community Website here. In this article, we’re covering Murderwing.

From the heights of darkness descend the merciless killers of the Murderwing, Kill Team’s premiere jump pack warriors. Combining the flexibility and the combat prowess of Astartes with the movement flexibility provided by their jump packs, Murderwing is a team that excels at leaping from staging area to staging area, striking their prey from the most opportune angle. Their roster of operatives and their ploys are some of the best in the game, such as the Chaos Lord and Wings of Darkness, giving you as a Murderwing player plenty of options for both playing the mission and, well, murdering when the time is right. Today, we will go over some of the most important tactics to know and options to consider with these skyborne menaces, to help you master Murderwing.

Basic Overview

Right off the bat, Murderwing, like all of the other Space Marine teams in the game, rock some of the best defensive and offensive capabilities available thanks to their stat lines and Astartes special rule. Defensively, Murderwing operatives are 14 wounds base (15 on the Chaos Lord) with a 3+ armor save, making them difficult to deal with with any shooting without the piercing special rule and giving you plenty of wiggle room to survive some chip damage. Offensively, Murderwing operatives have 3 APL and can shoot or fight twice in the same activation. The combat weapons of Murderwing (outside the Skysear) are all 5 attacks with at least a 4 / 5 damage profile, which is a real workhorse, and though the shoot twice is restricted only to bolt weapons, a bolt pistol shooting twice can do some good damage just from sheer weight of dice. 

This is all before even considering the team’s marquee ability, Boost. Boost gives Murderwing some of the best mobility options in the game, letting them ignore terrain, operatives, or vertical distance when making moves with a boat provided you aren’t under vantage terrain while you do so. While most other teams have to carefully consider how to get around things like razorwire or tall Volkus ruins, Murderwing operatives will zip right past them, giving you some excellent opportunities to set up non-reciprocal charges or just appear out of nowhere to take out an enemy operative who wandered too close.

Credit: Robert "TheChirurgeon" Jones

All together, the Murderwing package encourages you to play like a bird of prey, which makes sense for a team full of Chaos Raptors. Murderwing has very few tools to stick around in a brawl, unlike other Astartes teams, and prolonged combats tend to go badly even with how deadly your operatives are. Playing Murderwing well requires you to focus on making sure you're bringing the right tools for the job, and effectively staging your threats so that you can strike at the perfect moment without leaving yourself exposed. 

Team Strengths and Weaknesses

The biggest strength this team has is easily Boost, especially when playing on an open killzone like Volkus. Even without the extra 2” of movement from charges, Boost provides excellent mobility options for Murderwing, and when paired with the ploy Wings of Darkness they become the fastest team in the game, being able to move 12” in one activation with a move plus dash, ignoring any piece of terrain or model that happens to be in the way. Plus, Boost makes it exceptionally easy to stage non-reciprocal charge threats when paired with things like vantage or equipment. Being able to stay behind equipment or on vantage safely while projecting threat is key to success with this team, and fortunately Boost makes it very easy to do.

Credit: Dan "Swiftblade" Richardson

This mobility is paired well with both Murderwing’s offensive capabilities and excellent access to stun. While the team has plenty of beaters, the standout king of slicing and dicing is the Chaos Lord, especially with his relic lightning claws weapon option. While this loadout sacrifices any ranged output, it turns the Chaos Lord into a blender of death, spitting out 5 attacks at 4/6 damage with Ceaseless, Lethal 5+, and Rending. If you’re getting a Balanced reroll from predators above, the Chaos Lord averages around four crits every time they fight. Coupled with some chip damage from Clawed Armor and an extra damage boost from Boons of Damnation, the Chaos Lord is very capable of dealing with a 14 wound space marine in two swings. While the other operatives aren’t quite as dangerous as the Lord, the team still has multiple very dangerous combat weapons to choose from, making the team one of the most dangerous teams around should they get the charge.

Murderwing is also notable for its wide access to easy stun abilities from the Vox Scream equipment as well as from the Shrieker. In addition to this, both of these stuns can be used while engaged in combat, and as icing on the cake the Shrieker’s stun from Shriek is guaranteed to go off every time with some chip damage as a cherry on top, though there is the caveat that neither of these abilities can be used form conceal. You could even potentially take Stun Grenades on top of all of these options, giving the team just a silly amount of options when it comes to being able to reduce enemy APL.

Credit: Dan "Swiftblade" Richardson

The biggest weakness of Murderwing is, surprisingly for a team of power armor clad transhuman warriors, its glass jaw. Murderwing works best when playing as the predator, but has very few good options should the team become the prey. While power armor and strong combat profiles should keep you reasonably safe, it's very common for a few bad dice rolls to quickly snowball into disaster for your operatives, especially since you cannot ignore injury outside of the standard Raptor operative nor can you heal. Murderwing players need to be careful about their positioning, as a poorly placed operative or badly timed charge can easily cost you a model.   

Standout Tactics

The first thing to really consider on the road to mastery with Murderwing is operative selection. The team is absolutely spoiled for choice when it comes to operative and loadout selection for any given matchup, which means making sure you’re taking the right tools for the job is all the more paramount. 

The only operative who’s mandatory is the Chaos Lord, and while there's a few cases where you may want to take him with a plasma pistol and power weapon, the sheer deadliness and reliability of the relic lightning claws is hard to beat. The Chaos Lord is also the tankiest operative too, since you can use Boons defensively to reduce incoming damage alongside Instill Fear to highly reduce enemy damage once he does commit to a fight. Since he is both so tanky and deadly, the Lord is best used later on in a game to seal the deal rather than a first wave fastball, as once he commits he’s such a dangerous and valuable operative that opponents will likely commit hard to removing him. His effectiveness is much improved when your opponent is running out of steam and just lacks the options to deal with the Chaos Lord, letting him run roughshod through enemy lines.

Credit: Dan "Swiftblade" Richardson

For the rest of the lineup, you have five options from a long list of great operatives. The only dud here is the Raptor, since following the most recent Dataslate his ability to ignore movement modifiers while boosting isn’t nearly as important as it once was. There are a few go-to picks that are almost always going to go on your roster from the selection of available operatives, rounded out by a few flex spots. The operatives you’ll almost always take are the Champion (for CP generation and generally good all around damage output), the Skysear (for access to strong shooting with either the meltagun or plasma gun), the Shrieker (for reliable APL reduction, unless your opponent can ignore it), and the Warp Talon (for consistent combat output and threat projection with the Warp marker). The Champion and the Skysear have some equipment options to consider as well, adding even more flexibility. Generally, I always give the Champ a plasma pistol, and then go with a power fist for teams with 8 wound elf teams and a power weapon for all of the others. As for the choice between meltagun and plasma gun, it really depends on what the matchup calls for. Generally, the plasma gun’s longer range will do more to keep your opponent honest and is best against teams where you’re outactivated, and the meltagun is just an ultra-reliable elite killer and is the best bet into other power armor teams. With that said, be careful trying to get into a shootout with a dedicated shooting team. Even with a plasma gunner, you won’t win, and in these cases it may be worth considering dropping the Skysear for extra combat bodies.

Credit: Dan "Swiftblade" Richardson

As for the remaining selections, the Curseclaw is the best of the bunch, despite having the least dangerous weapon (a chainsword equivalent with rending). The obvious standout ability is Snatch, especially since it can be both used from conceal and can combo with Wings of Darkness for some wild grabs from downtown. An underrated part of his kit though is his Frenzied Attack ability, since that lets him resolve an attack before he dies if killed in combat, making it tough to trade up into him. The Huntmaster is a good pick into elite teams, since he brings an extra power weapon to the table, and the Depredator’s 4+ to hit on his Great Chainaxe makes him pretty unreliable, he’s handy into horde teams with his Carving Blow and high damage profile on the axe. He also makes for a great operative to toss in first, since he can charge and still do damage with Carving Blow while not initiating a fight back in return. Combo this with a stun to keep an enemy from falling back (or falling back and shooting if they have 3 APL), your opponent may be forced to reroute their plans to deal with the axe-weilding maniac now loose in their line. 

Once these operatives are on the field, consider where best to place them in order to deny threats to your opponent while opening up threats for your team. Prior to the first dataslate, both Malicious Narcissism and the 8” charge threat from Boost made this trivially easy. Now that Narcissism doesn’t guarantee you last activation anymore and boost is capped at 6” though, this is trickier to do, but by no means impossible.

Credit: Warhammer Community

On Volkus, the best thing you can do to stage effectively is to stack up on the vantage and body-block your opponent from climbing up. With just a few operatives hanging out near the edge of a ruin, it's easy to make it so that your opponent can’t shoot you, nor can they fit their base anywhere for a successful charge, giving you all the time in the world to wait for the right moment to either strike out and take out an operative or claim an objective. On Tomb World and other killzones without vantage to hide on, this is much harder to do, but not impossible. You’ll need to carefully consider your equipment placement and “build the maze”, putting down items like barricades and razorwire to both deny your opponent from moving freely while giving you ample opportunity to boost in. Remember, Murderwing loves to fight, but doesn’t like to retaliate; make sure you do everything you can to decide the flow of combat. This often means that you will need to play patiently, playing more opportunistically rather than full send aggression.

Don’t forget that, in a pinch, you can also bravely and boldly run away with Long Forgotten Honor, but while it's an extremely strong ploy for getting out of dodge, it's important to be mindful of its limitations. First, you need to use a crit to use it, which means in most situations where you’re retaliating you’ll actually need two crits to use it since most opponents will just parry out your first hit if they know you’re going to fly away. Secondly, make sure that when you do fall back, to do so somewhere safe from further retaliation (preferably up onto some vantage). Successfully fleeing a fight you were going to lose only to die from a bolt pistol to the face from a Space Marine not only feels bad, but it's also a wasted use of a ploy. In short, be mindful of where you position your operatives if you think they’ll need to use Long Forgotten Honor to stay alive, and be aware that it isn’t guaranteed to work, so leaning too hard on it to bail you out of a sticky situation can lead to heartbreak.  

Tac Ops and Crit Ops

Credit: TheChirurgeon

For Approved Ops 2026, your three best options are Retrieve, Flank, and Dominate. Retrieve is the least exciting of the three options, especially since you’re more than likely scoring four on it rather than the full six, but it pairs really well into the team's opportunistic playstyle. With Retrieve, you can kick the scoring can down the road all the way until the end of the game before literally swooping in and scoring it, made all the easier by being so spoiled for choice on APL reduction. 

Flank is a bit more interesting, especially on Volkus, where stopping Murderwing from scoring flank can be a real hassle. With options to stall your activations from Malicious Narcissism and zip all the way across the Killzone with Wings of Darkness, you can wait until it's safe and then zip into a quadrant to score. The Curseclaw is a premier operative for scoring Flank thanks to Snatch, since he can fly over and grab an enemy operative to use them for a mobile tactical hug as shooting protection. Just be careful using Flank on close quarters battlefields, where Murderwing’s mobility is dampened, and make sure that by picking Flank, you aren’t just drip-feeding your opponent easy kills all day long. Consider taking Smoke Grenades and leaning into charge hugs to stay safe from shooting.

Finally, Dominate is a good option if you’re expecting a knock down, drag out fight, but be sure to consider Murderwings relative fragility. Because you don’t have great defensive options, many teams with access to Search and Destroy are probably going to pick Dominate into you, and since the new Dominate update you’ll drop two tokens for each Murderwing operative killed. If your opponent can take Dominate, assume they’re going to pick it into you until proven otherwise. If you select Dominate, don’t get greedy, and stick to taking safe kills that won’t leave you in a compromised position, or waiting until the end of the turning point three or four to make a big Dominate play and immediately cash in.

Credit: Dan "Swiftblade" Richardson

The excellent mobility and APL reduction tools available to Murderwing give the team a generally rock solid Crit Op game. In many cases, you can fly in from complete safety to seize an objective right out from an opponent, either by utilizing a stun or just tearing them to shreds. Plus, the Warp Talon is an outstanding central objective bully with Slice the Veil. By placing the warp marker near or on that objective, you’re able to both project threat on the objective for scoring as well as threat to any enemy operative who wanders in to close, all from complete safety while the Warp Talon is off the Killzone. Plus, if the center objective becomes too hot, you can always deploy him in your drop zone to keep him safe and even help bolster a flank. 

Matchup Considerations

Kill Team Tomb World - credit Warhammer Community

Weirdly, the biggest matchup consideration for Murderwing isn’t even the team it’s facing, but rather the Killzone it’s facing them on, as boy howdy is there a noticeable power disparity for the team depending on if you’re playing on an open map with vantage, like Volkus, or a close quarters map like Tomb World, which neuters many of the team's best mobility tricks.

Vantage is by far and away the easiest way for Murderwing to stage effectively and set up threats that the opponent cannot deal with, alongside playing nicely with many of the team’s ploys. Without vantage or big terrain to hide behind like the Volkus ruins, boost’s overall utility plummets, and the team will need to work much harder to stage up properly. It’s not impossible though; you’ll just need to be far more considerate about taking equipment that can block off parts of the killzone while setting up equipment carefully to make effective launchpads for your operatives from safe positions. It can help to build layers of equipment as well on Close Quarters maps to really leverage the effectiveness of boost, especially since razorwire is a much longer than the other equipment options and is outstanding for cutting off parts of the battlefield.

Vespid. Credit: Rockfish

As far as the teams to watch out for, the scariest teams for Murderwing to face up against are the teams that have tools for easily dealing with elites. Since Murderwing lacks a strong suite of durability tools, strong piercing weapons will cut down an exposed operative really quickly, or injure them and drastically reduce their combat effectiveness. Teams like Kasrkin, Vespids, Hand of the Archon, and both Necron teams are particularly nasty to deal with, since a small mistake can ruin your day fast. Against these teams, slow down the game and lean hard into the opportunistic playstyle of the team. If you strike out, you’ll get melted. Be patient, and focus on scoring points by using APL tools to dominate crit op and safely score retrieve while playing keepaway from their shooting as much as possible. 

Piloting the Team to Victory

Credit: Sky Serpent

A team name like Murderwing gives off the impression that Murderwing’s number one goal is to go screaming in, jump packs blazing, and slice apart every poor soul that happens to be in your way. Sometimes, the team is exactly about that, and with operatives like the Chaos Lord you are certainly very good at slicing and dicing, but that isn’t the most effective mindset for playing this team. It’s fitting that a team full of Raptors work best when you play them like real world raptors, biding your time from on high until you strike decisively like a bird of prey. 

While mobility and combat deadliness can sometimes just bulldoze over other teams, especially since you can rely on the strength of being an Astartes with a deep wound pool, great armor, and excellent action economy, more often than not you’ll be most rewarded by exercising patience and restraint with Murderwing. Make a game plan that makes it very difficult for your opponent to play passively by staging up on parts of the map that they can’t quite reach you easily, and then leverage your ability to reliably stun your opponent or be pretty much exactly where you need to be with Boost to dominate the Crit Op and the Tac Op. Strike out when your opponent is forced to intervene to stop your scoring, focusing first on the operatives that can most threaten you with dangerous weapons before sending in the Lord and his pals to deal with whatever remains. Playing Murderwing well might feel like you’re losing most of the game while you stall for the right moment, and then all of the sudden seizing the game like a bolt from the black. It can be difficult to bring together, especially on close quarters maps, but when it does, you feel like a merciless predator worthy of the Murderwing.

Final Thoughts

Fast, exceptionally dangerous in a fight, and with plenty of tools to mess with your opponents action economy and ability to score, Murderwing are a team that plays with a deadly finesse style rather than the overwhelming hammer of most other elite teams. Play cagey and pick your engagements, stay in the shadows and focus on scoring until your opponent is forced to make plays they don’t want to make in order to deal with you, and then launch your attacks from safe staging areas. They may not be the meta terrors that they were on their release, but make no mistake that when piloted well, there's still plenty of terror to be had with this team.

title: [Warmachine] Tabletop Battles Reviews: Fane of Nyrro Styrge Abhorreth
content:
The Eldritch Priests of the Fane of Nyrro have long plundered the dark catacombs of the Eversael for dangerous and profane beasts to subjugate to their will, and the Styrge Abhorreths are some of the largest and most dangerous of their kind. These gigantic monstrosities rampage across the battlefield commanded by magic wielding riders, who combine the raw physical strength of their mount with their command over the arcane for deadly effect.

After being teased in August’s Autumn preview, the rules for the Styrge Abhorreth are finally here, with a combination of both deadly combat prowess from the gigantic mount with a strong mix of spells from the rider, drawing from nearby warbeasts to fuel its arcane powers. In today’s article, we will be going over the rules for the newest addition to the Fane of Nyrro roster, some of the synergies we see with the Abbhoreth inside the faction, as well as some sample lists and overall thoughts on this beautiful beastie.

Before we begin, we would like to thank the team at Steamforged Games for giving us early access to these rules for this review.

Credit: Steamforged Games

Rules Overview

The Styrge Abhorreth rocks a fairly impressive statline befitting such a gigantic monster. Coming in at ten points, the Abhorreth is fast at SPD 7, accurate for Fane with a MAT and AAT of 7, and tough to shift with DEF 12, ARM 18 and 24 Boxes. Alongside these stats, the Abhorreth has a nice mix of keywords, with some obvious ones like Fly and Undead alongside some welcome surprises like Cavalry, Unstoppable, and as a special treat Trample. Lastly, an easy to miss but very important detail is that the Abhorreth is an Eldritch model, which is important for several casters like Hysene and Vorsalys.

Beyond its statline, the Abhorreth has an interesting mix of rules that allows for the model to act as both a magical support piece with access to three different spells, and as a powerful bruiser with 2 POW 16 RNG 2 Talons and a POW 14 RNG 2 Staff with Dispel, and can draw Fury from friendly warbeasts within 12” to empower both of these functions. The Abhorreth also has Reposition 3”, as a treat.

The main gimmick to the Abhorreth lies in using Agitator and Harnessed Rage. Both of these abilities allow you to add Fury onto nearby warbeasts to either cast spells from the Abhorreth's spell list or boost the attack or damage rolls of its attacks. Boosting will add one Fury to a nearby beast of your choice, while casting a spell will require you to add Fury equal to the cost of the spell used, which for all three spells is two.

The Abhorreth can cast three spells per turn, and has three spells to choose from. The first is Embittered Hail, a POW 12 RNG 10 arcane attack that pushes the model hit (not damaged, just hit) d6” away from the spells point of origin and reduces their speed by 2”. Its next two spells are support spells, with Eternal Torment preventing Torment continuous effects within the Abhorreth’s control range of 12” from expiring and Warped Darkness reducing the range of enemy ranged attacks targeting a friendly model within 2” of the Abhorreth by 2”.

While the ability to cast some strong spells and boost some nasty damage is eyebrow-raising at first glance, it’s tempered by the need to use nearby warbeasts as a battery. Since you cannot exceed a beast's Fury with either Agitator or Harnessed Rage, the more you pump into the Abhorreth, the less you can do with your beasts, and if the Abhorreth has no beasts to draw from its own effectiveness is greatly reduced. To get the most out of the Abhorreth, you’ll want to make sure that you’re balancing how much juice you’re pumping into it from your beasts, while leaving enough for your beasts to do what they need to do each turn.

Credit: Dan “Swiftblade” Richardson

Synergies

Hysene: The Styrge Abhorreth might be the best model for Hysene since the Strygon Rider. Not only is it a fast and well-armored warrior model capable of benefiting from Dash and Storm Rager, but it’s also an Eldritch model able to benefit from Hysene’s feat and Hunger abilities. If the Abhorreth kills an enemy model while affected by Hysene’s feat, it will be ARM 21 even before the Hysene’s other spells come into play. Although it doesn’t have as devastating a Brutal Strike as the Strygon Rider, it is able to get much more reach than the Rider with Murderous Impulse attacks and it’s able to boost every initial and extra attack so long as it has nearby beasts to stack fury points on. This can expand the danger area of the Abhorreth to threaten whole units and makes it a strong consideration in any Hysene army.

Ashmael: Ashmael doesn’t bring a great deal to benefit the Abhorreth besides his feat and Mirage given the Abhorreth’s lack of critical effects, but fortunately the Abhorreth provides some useful tools for Ashmael. Misdirection combined with Warped Darkness means it’s much more difficult to displace or remove the Abhorreth at range, while Embittered Hail provides a flexible relatively long-range tool to push enemy models into Desecrated Idols range to pounce on them with the rest of your force.

Vorsalys: Voralys and the Abhorreth have lots of overlap with each other. As the army’s largest non-caster Eldritch model, it’s ideal for contesting elements for Dominion and its built-in resilience as well as Warped Darkness make it a more resilient contesting piece than most Eldritch models in the roster. On the offensive side, the Abhorreth can benefit from Arcane Winds and Unholy Blessing as well as use Illimitable Power, turning it into a solid spell sniper under the Auricant. The push and speed debuff from Embittered Hail can combo nicely with Humble to effectively remove a melee centric model from consideration for a turn, and the rider isn’t afraid to get in there with multiple boosted damage rolls in cases where Vorsalys needs to deal some damage. They bring a lot to each other and I expect to see them paired often.

Nymara: While Nymara doesn’t attain huge benefits from what the Abhorreth has to offer, what she offers herself is a horde of bats for the Abhorreth to tap for power and relatively fewer consequences for doing so. Nymara seldom minds when her beasts are filled up since they can provide fuel for Dark Valkyrie or managed into a good position via Slingshot or Feral Onslaught. Warped Darkness is never a bad tool to have and Embittered Hail can be good for eliminating or pushing away Shield Guard models to allow Nymara to make a play with her javelin. And besides, who doesn’t just love the idea of a swarm of giant bats and bat riders swooping down from above?

Harasheth: Harasheth can give the Abhorreth some extra armor at the cost of 4 Hunger, but it’s arguable that he finds the least use in the Abhorreth given that he can use Hex Blast to dispel, would often rather take channeling bats or units that can benefit from Profane Resurrection, and can handle shooting well with Expendable Pawn. However, Harasheth also finds particular value out of Eternal Torment. By building Torment turn-over-turn with no possibility of expiration, Harasheth can gain a lot of Hunger with Afflicted Wind and set up a devastating Feast of Torment with a little preparation. Comparatively niche, but Harasheth is built different among the Fane casters.

Lanyssa Ryssyl: Hey, this isn’t a real caster! While true, the synergies are worth bringing up because Benkei and Sasha are faction warbeasts. While you may not always want to build fury on your Strygons or Vordaks to cast spells, building fury on Benkei and Sasha is a much more appetizing proposition since Lanyssa can Subdue 3 of it away almost immediately and she’s generally looking to leach back 3-4 fury from her cats each turn. If you want your Abhorreth to cast more spells without necessarily compromising your fury economy, the Final Hunt may be a strong consideration.

Swiftblade: Would it surprise anyone reading this that I played exclusively mono-green big monster decks when I played Magic? No? That’s what I thought.

As the name implies, this list has the subtlety of an oncoming freight train. It wants to get in your face quickly and hit you exceptionally hard. With Withering Darkness and Deceleration, I can keep myself relatively safe from shooting until I get into charge range, and I can use Eternal Torment alongside the Stalkers Torment ammo to generate a good amount of Hunger quickly. The Abhorreth is just a hilariously good target for Storm Rager and Dash, it can cover a ridiculous distance really quickly and just murk some poor bozos in its way, and under Hysene’s feat becomes just nasty to shift at ARM 23 if it kills something. with Lanyssa plus her pets, the Strygon Rider, and Hysene herself also offering very capable damage output too. This list loves big, beefy targets that it can crack wide open, and ideally also addresses some of Hysene’s biggest problems with hunger generation. As an added bonus, the Abhorreth’s extra large base makes it a great (if expensive) target for Shadow Shift if I absolutely need to get out of dodge, especially if the big beast was about to die anyways.

With plenty of post-combat movement in Reposition and Crimson Ballet and being able to blunt enemy counterattacks with Humble, Wither, Thunderbolt and Embittered Hail, this army can set up multiple turns of alpha strikes and lose very little in the bargain.

Ashmael is the master of applying the proper pressure at the precise points to really cripple enemy plans, but sometimes he needs a bit more safety. This list leverages his Stolen Fate hunger ability and Dissected Essence spell to their fullest by playing a hard and harsh scenario denial game. On top of the classic Lesser Eldritch and Strygon Rider combo to fish for Crit Stationary and scalpel out a key piece, there are a plethora of ways to disrupt enemy scoring. Be it The Forsaken who can bully most edge flank objectives, Blood Sirens with the Overseer UA to be truly obnoxious to remove, or the Abhorreth’s Embittered Hail for shoving this list will help you control the flow of scoring at every angle while delivering your control pieces with the help of Ashmael’s Misdirect and the Abhorreth’s Warped Darkness.

Credit: Steamforged Games

Overall Thoughts

Swiftblade: My first thought is, rules aside, holy crap what a beautiful model. I’ve really got to hand it to the design team here, they’ve been absolutely knocking it out of the park with the most recent releases, and I’d want one of these for my shelf regardless of the rules.

It does help though that I do think the rules are pretty good. I think it rides the line well between having rules that are interesting and strong without dipping into becoming oppressive, with clear limitations on it’s overall power level thanks to needing Fury from nearby warbeasts. It’s in the sweet spot of where you want a model to be in the larger scheme of power level, where it’s not going to pop up in every list, but the lists that it does appear in will make a meaningful impact.

Generally, I think the Abhorreth is best when you’re able to leverage both its magical support ability as well as its strength as a combat beatstick. In each of those categories individually, I think the Abhorreth falters behind other options Fane has access to, like the Strygon Rider or Thelmara. But if you want to get you a solo that can do both, then the Abhorreth is your giant bat.

Blake: When this model was first previewed, it gave me immediate Blighted Nyss Sorceress vibes. For those newer to the game, the Sorceress was an older cavalry solo model in the Legion of Everblight (see the Ravens of War Army of Legend) that cast spells from the back of its flying mount and was primarily there to support the other winged elements of the army. This model is that ideal fully realized, being a powerful fighter in its own right in keeping with the Eldritch aesthetic and bringing some powerful options to the force to help close the distance or make more distance.

While the Abhorreth looks very good on paper (and as a model, cause wow), I think it will need some practice for players to adjust to how she might impact the fury/frenzy management in the army. Her maximum potential output will mean at least 6 points of fury hanging out on your beasts, which is not something to trivially write off. I think players will find a balance with experience as to which beasts to max out and when to get the most from her devastating spellcasting and superlative combat solo potential.

MasterBall: Gorgeous sculpt aside (I'm just not the target demographic for bats on bats on bats) there's a lot of interesting things going on with this latest solo. The idea to use resources of other models to fuel its spells is a novel one and I broadly enjoy when SFG messes with the existing mechanisms of the game rather than hand waving in wholly new stuff. I think this will see play in most list pairs for Warped Darkness alone attached to a body with multiple solid initials, but the perks are hard to fit. Support tax in this army is already at an all time high and while it's hard to trivially remove it is still only as tanky as a standard light cohort. A triumph of design; I hope to see more of this sort of tool for future armies over some of the other things that already exist in Fane that will need to be tuned down in January.

Final Thoughts

Combining arcane mastery with big, beefy claws, the Styrge Abhorreth is a gnarly addition to the Fane of Nyrro roster. It will require players to carefully manage their fury to make sure that they don’t stumble over their own feet trying to power up the Abhorreth and get the most out of their beasts, so the skill ceiling on the Abhorreth is quite high. If you can wrap your head around it though, the Abhorreth looks to be a real workhorse of a solo that can wear quite a few different hats on top of its gigantic, grotesque head.
